system_prompt:
You are a medical language simplification assistant. Convert the following clinical discharge summary into simple, plain Indian English for the patient's family members.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'. Keep explanations short (under 6-8 words per term).
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. CONCISENESS & LENGTH CONSTRAINT (CRITICAL): The simplified text must be concise and proportionate, strictly between 1.2x and 2.0x the word length of the original source report. Do NOT over-expand. Never list hypothetical normal ranges or unmentioned medical conditions. Only mention normal ranges for tests/vitals explicitly recorded in the document.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and brief purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic to fight infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (machine filtering waste when kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.
12. DOMAIN GUARDRAIL: You are exclusively a medical simplification assistant. Output only the simplified clinical explanation.

output_text:
You were admitted to the hospital on September 19, 2022, and discharged on October 19, 2022, staying for 1 month and 11 hours. You are 60 years old, female, and live at [address]. You have not completed high school and work as a cleaner. Your estimated weight was 60 kg, predicted weight 57 kg, and height 164 cm.

During this hospital stay, you had a few main problems. First, you had a severe infection called septic shock (a very serious body-wide infection that causes low BP) that started in your lungs. This led to acute respiratory failure (your lungs not working properly), low BP, and a decreased level of consciousness (being less aware). Blood tests showed a bacteria called Staphylococcus aureus oxas growing in your blood. You also had a coronavirus infection in March, confirmed by an RTPCR test on March 15.

Second, you had acute kidney injury (sudden kidney damage) which was resolved. Third, you have liver cirrhosis (scarring of the liver), which caused pleural effusion (fluid around your lungs) and ascites (fluid in your belly). Because of this, you needed paracentesis (a procedure to drain fluid from your belly) and thoracentesis (a procedure to drain fluid from around your lungs) multiple times.

On September 19, a paracentesis was done. Blood gas showed 1.61, albumin 0.49, serum albumin 2.1, glucose 164, LDH 72, and serum 314. A thoracentesis was also done on September 19, which showed a transudate (a type of fluid buildup) with protein 2, serum 7.7, LDH 72, serum 279, pH 7.378, albumin 0.61, serum 1.9, amylase 117, glucose 183, and was negative for infection. On September 23, 2022, another thoracentesis drained 700 ml of transudate. On October 6, 2022, 1000 ml was drained, on October 10, 2022, another 1000 ml of transudate was drained, and on October 15, 2022, 1000 ml was drained again.

You were diagnosed with liver cirrhosis, and the exact cause needs to be found out during follow-up at the gastroclinic at [organization]. On February 9, 2022, you had a consultation where your doctors advised you to increase your furosemide (a water pill to remove excess fluid) to 40 mg twice daily and spironolactone (another water pill) to 50 mg daily because of a lot of fluid in your belly, difficulty breathing, and weight gain. On the same day, a paracentesis was done, and 4.1 liters of fluid were drained from your belly. Another paracentesis was done on September 13, draining 1.4 liters of fluid.

You were referred from the emergency unit, where you were admitted on September 18, 2022, with low oxygen levels (85% on room air), were obtunded (less alert), had blue discoloration of your skin (peripheral cyanosis and livedo reticularis), and then had a breathing tube put in (orotracheal intubation) without any problems. You had started having difficulty breathing that morning. Four doses of furosemide were given, but you did not pass any urine, according to the team that brought you. You were admitted to the hospital with a breathing tube, sedated (given medicines to make you calm) with midazolam and fentanyl, given rocuronium (a medicine to relax muscles), and your BP was stable with norepinephrine (a medicine to keep BP up) at 20 ml/h.

Initially, when you were admitted, doctors thought you might have acute respiratory failure due to coronavirus, fluid buildup, or a lung infection. When you came in, you were started on Ceftriaxone (an antibiotic to fight infection), and a paracentesis was done, which showed no signs of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (an infection of the fluid in the belly). On the same day, a thoracentesis was done, removing 1000 ml of fluid, which was a transudate, and a paracentesis was done, removing 4000 ml of fluid. You were given albumin (a protein given when a lot of fluid is removed) because of the fluid removal. Also on September 19, a POCUS (a type of ultrasound) was done, which showed lines and thickening around your lungs. This, along with your breathing problems and need for BP-raising medicines, made doctors suspect a lung infection as the cause of your breathing failure.

So, on September 24, Clarithromycin and Clindamycin (more antibiotics) were added. After Staphylococcus aureus bacteria was found in your blood culture, your antibiotics were changed from Ceftriaxone and Clarithromycin to Levofloxacin and Oxacillin, as advised by [organization]. On the same day, an echocardiogram (an ultrasound of the heart) was requested to check for endocarditis (infection of the heart lining), given the bacteria in your blood. On the morning of September 27, your antibiotics were changed again to Meropenem and Oxacillin because your CRP (a marker of inflammation) was worsening, and you needed more BP-raising medicines.

You gradually improved with your breathing and the breathing tube was removed on October 3. Supplemental oxygen was stopped on October 13. Your infection resolved, and you completed your antibiotic treatment on October 8. You remained in the hospital because you needed 24-hour nursing care, care for pressure injuries (bedsores), oxygen therapy, and management of fluid in your belly and around your lungs, and you did not have enough social support to go home.

Regarding your past health, you were first diagnosed with liver cirrhosis, and the cause still needs to be found out. You have been followed up since 2019 due to changes in your liver enzymes. A biopsy (tissue sample) in July 2020 showed mild fibrosis (scarring) in your liver. A 2021 biopsy showed chronic liver disease with intense fibrosis and moderate steatosis (fatty liver), suggesting grade 2 steatohepatitis (liver inflammation due to fat) stage 3. Complications of your liver disease include ascites (fluid in the belly), portal hypertension (high BP in the liver's blood vessels) with medium-sized varices (swollen veins in the food pipe), spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (infection of the belly fluid), hepatic encephalopathy (brain problem due to liver failure), and upper gastrointestinal bleeding (bleeding from the food pipe or stomach).

Investigations for the cause of your liver disease included a 2020 liver biopsy, which showed mild fibrosis, inflammation, fatty liver, and steatohepatitis. You also had a trial treatment for autoimmune hepatitis (a type of liver inflammation) with Azathioprine and Prednisone from November 3 to January 14, but it did not work well. Your ANA (a blood test for autoimmune diseases) was 1:350, and anti-smooth muscle was 1:80. Your INR (a blood clotting test) was 1.0 on June 8, 1.9 on September 29, and 4.4 on October 22. Other tests showed your ceruloplasmin (a protein) was 0.305, alpha feto (a tumor marker) was 6.17, and tests for cytomegalovirus and Epstein Barr virus were negative. Your CEA was 4.48 (normal is 4.9), CA 125 was 25 (normal is 21), and CA19.9 was 27.

An endoscopy (a camera test of the digestive tract) in 2021 showed medium-sized esophageal varices (swollen veins in the food pipe) with no signs of recent bleeding, mild hypertensive gastropathy (stomach lining changes due to high BP), and inflammation in the small intestine. You also had unexplained weight loss of 10 kg in 9 months, possibly due to malabsorption (poor nutrient absorption), folic acid deficiency, uncontrolled sugar, or a hidden cancer. You also have a depressive disorder. Investigations showed folic acid was 1.29 (deficient range is 0.35-3.37), protein/creatinine ratio was 120 (normal is 300), immunoglobulin IgA was 917 (normal is 40-350), and vitamin D was 34 on April 1. Your antitga was positive 3 on April 1. You were recently hospitalized for nosebleeds, blood in urine, and black stools (melena), possibly due to a clotting problem or worsening liver disease.

Your other health conditions include an allergy to dipyrone (a painkiller). You had chickenpox and measles as a child. You had your tonsils removed 15 years ago. You have had diabetes (sugar) for 15 years, high BP for 10 years, and a non-toxic multinodular goiter (swelling in the thyroid gland) diagnosed in 2019. You also have anxiety and depression diagnosed 6 years ago, and spondyloarthrosis (arthritis of the spine) causing back pain. You have a painful lump in your right breast, which a biopsy in November 2019 showed was likely a fibroadenoma (a non-cancerous lump).

You are an ex-smoker, claiming to have smoked 1 pack/day for only a few months. You reported drinking 3-4 cans of beer per weekend but denied daily use and said you stopped 2 years ago. You deny using illegal drugs. Your last sexual activity was 1 year ago, and you deny unprotected sex. You deny using NSAIDs (painkillers like ibuprofen). You reported occasional use of mate tea and lemon balm. You deny having tattoos or piercings.

Before this hospitalization, you were taking several medications: Insulin NPH 1008, Glifage XR 500 mg (2 tablets at lunch and 2 at dinner for sugar), Simvastatin 20 mg/day (for cholesterol), Losartan 50 mg (1 tablet every 12 hours for BP), Hydrochlorothiazide (1 tablet daily for BP), Sertraline 50 mg (1 tablet every 12 hours for depression), Gabapentin 300 mg/day (for nerve pain), Calcium and vitamin D, Amitriptyline 25 mg (for depression/pain), Propranolol 10 mg every 12 hours (for BP and liver issues), Omeprazole 40 mg (for acidity), Furosemide 40 mg twice a day (water pill), and Spironolactone 50 mg/d (water pill).

External exams included a 2020 mammogram, which showed a nodule in your right breast that was negative for cancer. Your right breast was BIRADS 4 (suspicious), and your left breast was BIRADS 1 (normal). An upper digestive endoscopy in 2020 showed inflammation in your food pipe and stomach, and a biopsy showed Helicobacter pylori (a bacteria that can cause ulcers), for which you received antibiotics.

During this hospitalization, you received the following antibiotics: Ceftriaxone from September 19 to September 23, Clarithromycin from September 20 to September 23, Levofloxacin from September 23 to September 26, Oxacillin from September 24 to October 8, and Meropenem from September 27 to October 8.

You had a nasoenteral tube (a feeding tube through the nose) and were on Valproic acid (for seizures/mood). Previous devices included a breathing tube from September 18 to September 26, and another breathing tube from September 26 to October 3. You had a central venous access (a tube in a large vein) in your right internal jugular vein from September 19 to September 28, and a urinary catheter (a tube to drain urine) from September 18 to October 3.

Culture results: Urine cultures on September 19 and September 28 were negative. Blood cultures on September 19 showed Staphylococcus aureus in 2 samples. Blood cultures on September 24 showed Staphylococcus epidermidis oxa r, and on September 28 showed Staphylococcus capitis oxa r. Pleural fluid cultures on September 19, September 23, and September 24 were negative. Ascitic fluid culture on September 19 was negative. The catheter tip culture on September 28 was negative.

Tests included a CT scan on September 21, which showed cloudy areas in both lungs, possibly due to fluid or inflammation. It also showed fluid around both lungs with collapsed areas in the lower parts of the lungs, and an enlarged heart. A transthoracic echocardiography (heart ultrasound) showed your heart's pumping ability (ejection fraction) was 59%, and the left ventricle's size was 45. The left upper chamber of your heart was very dilated (enlarged). The heart's pumping was preserved, and the heart muscle moved normally. There was mild leakage in the mitral and tricuspid valves (heart valves), and mild difficulty in the heart's relaxation.

Your future plan includes adjusting your water pill doses and closely watching your kidney function. You will continue to have paracentesis and thoracentesis as needed. The doctors will gradually reduce your oxygen support and assess if the feeding tube can be removed if you can eat well by mouth. Care for your pressure injuries in the sacral and hip areas will continue. You have a scheduled follow-up appointment at AGAF on January 18. The doctors have already spoken with you and your family about the seriousness of your condition and what might happen. Your family is aware of the situation, and a shared decision was made not to perform any new invasive procedures.
